title: Reward for Objection
paragraphs: The Tamiḻ professor made an announcement in the classroom of the college: “Students, I announce a competition to commemorate the birth anniversary of the Tamiḻ scholar Thiru V. Ka. The best among you who scene scripts a characterizing a man and a woman in a beautiful manner, in sweet, charming Tamiḻ by conforming to the established rules of old Tamiḻ tradition and history would bag a prize of literature books worth rupees five thousand. Well then! You can as well start now and read out your work to me before the end of this class”.
The students welcomed this announcement and raced against each other to write the script in order to bag the prize.
“There is yet another condition for winning the competition! You should finish it first, and further your work should be prize-worthy.”
Within an hour of the announcement, Mukilaṉ finished his work and he approached the professor with the papers. He said, “Sir, I have finished writing.”
“Is that so! I am quite happy! Why don’t you read it aloud to others?”
Student Mukilaṉ started rushing through with his presentation:
The lover sits by his beloved wearing a sad countenance.
She enquires, “Why are you sorrow-worn? Why does your face look withered?”
“Sulking”, is the crisp reply.
“Sulking? What does it mean...?”

“O my goodness! You don’t know what sulking means! Among the verses in Iṉpattuppāl section of Tirukkuṟaḷ, those under “sulking” are the best. The man and woman have a feigned quarrel against each other, which ultimately gets resolved leading to ecstasy.”
“In the first place, why should they sulk and then settle down to reconciliation?”
“Sulking is entering into a quarrel with the sole aim of getting reconciled.”
“Okay then, what are you waiting for? Start the quarrel.”
“I am going to break a piece of news, most disliked by you.”
“What is it?”
“The dawn tomorrow would see me sailing to Rome.”
“Oh, no. Don’t tell me you are off to a foreign land once again.”
“Yes, we need to carry the pearls of Tamiḻ Nāṭu for sale in Rome.”
“Alas! Was I born to be tossed like a catamaran by the ebb and tide of the sea waves? No, I am determined to stop your voyage.”
“No obstacles please! Let there be no embers in your eyes! If I sell pearls overseas, gold coins would pile like a flood unshuttered. So dear lady, let me take leave of you.”
“When I, like the lamp of the house, wait for you here with my fingers crossed, you tear apart the tumultuous sea to go for trading. I would have breathed my last by the time you returned.”

“Come on! Look here! You are soon going to break into pearls of laughter, which certainly doesn’t grow in the shell. Oh chaste Tamiḻ, which abide in my heart! You are going to accompany me to Rome. Is that okay?”
After hearing this sweet news she planted some mighty kisses and embraced her lord.
Everybody in the classroom appreciated Mukilaṉ with a thunderous applause.
The Tamiḻ professor said, “What students? Shall we confer the first prize on Mukilaṉ? But one thing. This script doesn’t completely belong to Mukilaṉ.
It reads like part of a dialogue in the play Pūmpukār!”
Student Mullaikkoṭi intervened: “Professor sir! Friend Mukilaṉ’s work doesn’t conform to the norms of ancient Tamiḻ literature and culture. Nor is it completely like the dialogue in Pūmpukār.”
“What is your objection? If you could reflect what is in my mind, you will get the prize.”
“Sir, last week while teaching Tolkāppiyam, you explained the Akattiṇai iyal
verse 34 as meaning that the ancient Tamiḻ culture did not permit men taking their wives with them during voyages to foreign lands. And what Mukilaṉ has written runs contrary to this practice.”

“Yes Mullaikkoṭi! You have said exactly what I thought. Dear Mukilaṉ, your script is excellent! The pen-portrait you have done remains a feast for the eyes! But then, the award should rightly go to the objection raised by Mullaikkoṭi!
Once again, the students expressed their happiness by their clapping of hands.
> The hero does not take the heroine with him > While he undertakes a voyage on the seas. > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 34).
